findings.claim: PSM submap analysis lets the group 'extract targeted leverage-point submaps'
findings.failure_mode: Source vocabulary loosened: submaps focus on 'particular questions or issues'; 'leverage point' is not the source's concept and implies a claim about intervention potency the source does not make
findings.evidence: Deep 139 ('a way in, to what can be an overwhelmingly large diagram'; stakeholder- or system-suggested starting points); source 3426-3448
findings.fix: correct: extract targeted submaps around particular questions or issues

findings.claim: "Rich Pictures are a drawing, a picture, of a system or 'situation'. Very few, if any, prompts are given by facilitators beyond asking them to 'draw the system.'"
findings.failure_mode: Two non-contiguous source sentences stitched into one quotation with no ellipsis and a recapitalised 'Very'; no evidence marker on text presented as the author's words
findings.evidence: Deep 79 carries them as two separate [V] fragments; source 1513 and 1519-1520 are several sentences apart ('...what the picture should contain is often left completely up to the participants; very few, if any, prompts...')
findings.fix: re-mark: [V], and split into two quotations or insert '...' and restore lowercase 'very'

findings.claim: CLDs sit "roughly in the middle of the qualitative-quantitative spectrum ... but hints at dynamics in a system."
findings.failure_mode: Verbatim author quotation carried without [V] marker

findings.claim: Participatory maps become "boundary objects around which stakeholders and researchers can learn."
findings.failure_mode: Quotation silently elides '(see Star & Griesemer, 1989)' between 'boundary objects' and 'around which'; no marker; the borrowed-through concept is not flagged [BT] in-line
findings.evidence: Deep 255 ([V] [BT]); source 6834-6835: "The maps become 'boundary objects' (see Star & Griesemer, 1989) around which stakeholders and researchers can learn."
findings.fix: correct: become 'boundary objects' (see Star & Griesemer, 1989) "around which stakeholders and researchers can learn" [V] [BT]

findings.claim: 'The appropriateness gate (the broken-ankle test equivalent)': the book's consistent stance is that systems-mapping methods are 'gateway tools' for complex causal questions, not universal tools; when the incident is simple and the fix obvious, formal mapping is not warranted (Ch 1, 'How Can Systems Mapping Be Useful?')
findings.failure_mode: Concept imported from another source and attributed to this one. The broken-ankle test is SSDL Brief 1.02's Adam Raney quote, not Barbrook-Johnson & Penn. 'Gateway tools' in this source means entry-point tools for engaging with complexity ('ways to start engaging with real-world complex systems'), not a scoping gate. The 'do not map simple incidents' stance is absent from the deep ref. Section also mis-cited. The concept anchor `broken-ankle-test` will route concept-index lookups to this source.
findings.evidence: Deep 69 cites 'gateway' to Ch 1 'Why Think About Systems Mapping Now?'; source 1276 (heading) and 1309-1315; ssdl-systems-thinking-foundations-deep 23, 55 (broken-ankle quote, Brief 1.02 '+CONSIDERATIONS')
findings.fix: strip (the concept and its anchor); if a scoping caveat is wanted, cite this source's own limit: emergent effects 'need other modelling approaches' (Ch 1, 'Why Think About Systems Mapping Now?') [V], and point to SSDL in the integration table for the broken-ankle test

findings.claim: The core system engine is 'the two or three feedback loops at the centre of the event'
findings.failure_mode: Definition attached to the wrong element and a count invented: the core system engine is a set of central nodes/variables (one defining variable or a handful), around which loops are focused; no 'two or three loops' figure in the source
findings.evidence: Deep 115; source 2793-2795 ('a set of nodes that are the core of the system'), 2914-2919 ('one defining variable at the centre ... or a handful of key variables')
findings.fix: correct: Start with the core system engine (the one or handful of central variables that drive the system's behaviour) and the feedbacks around it

findings.claim: 'Which causal links go in both directions?'
findings.failure_mode: CLD links carry polarity (positive = move together, negative = move in opposite directions); 'go in both directions' suggests bidirectional links, a feature the source does not describe
findings.fix: correct: Which links are positive (the variables move together) and which negative (they move in opposite directions)?

findings.claim: To 'identify the highest-leverage points', run a submap analysis: which factors have the most connections, which sit on paths between consequential inputs and outcomes (Ch 5)
findings.failure_mode: Source's system-suggested starting points (centrality, bridging) are for choosing where a submap starts because they 'might have interesting properties', not for identifying leverage
findings.fix: correct: Need = 'The group wants a principled place to start focused analysis'; keep the centrality and path questions as submap starting points

findings.claim: Prioritise actions by 'which actions address factors with high centrality? Favour actions that intervene on the core system engine over those that address peripheral nodes' (Ch 5, 'What Is Participatory Systems Mapping?')
findings.failure_mode: Prioritisation rule the source does not give, attributed to Ch 5; 'core system engine' is the Ch 4 CLD concept, not a PSM term; the source does not equate centrality with action priority
findings.evidence: Deep 139-141 (Ch 5 submap starting points and rules), 115 and 123 (Ch 4 core engine; 'Disrupting a vicious cycle or encouraging a virtuous one is probably the most intuitive way...')
findings.fix: correct: Which candidate actions would disrupt a vicious cycle or strengthen a virtuous one in the map? (Ch 4, "Commons Issues and 'Tricks of the Trade'"); use a submap around each candidate's factor to see what it drives downstream (Ch 5)

findings.claim: 'If the system structure did not change, the same event will recur' (Ch 4, "Common Issues and 'Tricks of the Trade'")
findings.failure_mode: Embedded premise (structure determines recurrence) is not in the deep ref and is cited to a section that discusses loop-thinking care, button-pushing mindsets and vicious/virtuous cycles
findings.fix: strip the premise sentence; keep 'Was the prior action addressing the event or the loop?' as applied guidance

findings.claim: Do not reach for this source when the incident is simple and the fix is obvious ('the broken-ankle test applies')
findings.failure_mode: Uses another corpus source's named concept (SSDL Brief 1.02) without attribution, reading as this source's gate
findings.evidence: ssdl-systems-thinking-foundations-deep 55; Barbrook-Johnson deep has no such test
findings.fix: correct: ... (SSDL's broken-ankle test, Brief 1.02, applies: formal mapping is not warranted)

findings.claim: 'The facilitator applies the submap technique (Ch 5) to extract the two highest-centrality factors ... as the leverage points'
findings.failure_mode: Misdescribes the submap technique (a submap is generated from a chosen starting factor by upstream/downstream, ego-network or path rules) and presents centrality-as-leverage as the framework's move
findings.fix: correct: uses network measures to pick system-suggested starting points (scope-change rate, resource-reallocation latency) and draws one-to-two-step upstream/downstream submaps around them to see what drives them and what they drive

findings.claim: SSDL 'provides the system-archetype vocabulary ... that gives this source's CLD seed structures their names; use SSDL to select the archetype hypothesis'
findings.failure_mode: This source names all eight archetypes itself (via Kim 2000); SSDL covers five (via Kim 1993) with template definitions and worked examples. SSDL also cautions against 'jumping in to use archetypes when facilitating a group model building workshop', which the integration row omits
findings.fix: correct: Shared lineage (Kim). This source lists eight archetypes as CLD core-engine seeds; SSDL gives template definitions and worked examples for five, and warns that jumping to archetypes in a group session can reinforce an expert-vs-novice dynamic

findings.claim: 'The Barbrook-Johnson & Penn text itself is a secondary-source catalogue'
findings.failure_mode: Mischaracterises the source: Ch 5 presents the authors' own method (PSM), developed by them over ten years, and Chs 9-12 carry their own practice positions
findings.fix: correct: The text is largely a methods overview, but Ch 5 (PSM) is the authors' own method; its borrowed-through chain is extensive and recorded in the deep ref

findings.claim: 'The appropriateness-triangle quotation is [V] in the deep ref; the distillation paraphrases it in Concept 1'
findings.failure_mode: Continuity note is wrong (Concept 1 quotes it verbatim with [V]) and omits the three unmarked quotations in Concepts 2, 6 and 11
findings.fix: correct: Concept 1 carries the appropriateness quotation as [V]; Concepts 2, 6 and 11 quote [V] passages and should carry the marker

notes: Integration rows for LFUO (networked causality, Five Hows), Org Topologies (MAP step) and TC 25-20 (chronological / BOS / key events) and the NHS reference in Named Limits all check out against their deep refs. Kim 2000 'Systems Archetypes I' title is correct per the source bibliography (line 3232) though not in the deep ref. The worked example is clearly hypothetical and asserts no outcome as the source's finding, but it carries no verbatim blockquote (protocol asks for one where the source's words carry the claim) and has three people each draw an individual picture where the source's default is small groups drawing one shared picture (individual use noted only as a minority suggestion). Recurring pattern: centrality / core-engine recast as 'leverage points' across lines 8, 53, 62, 93.
